title: Japanese Companies Exit China in Record Numbers as India Emerges as Alternative
excerpt: Teikoku Databank counts 10,118 Japanese companies in mainland China, down 30% from the 2012 peak, as firms shift investment toward India and Southeast Asia.
body:
• Teikoku Databank reports 10,118 Japanese companies had a presence in mainland China as of June 2026 — the lowest since it began tracking the data in 2010, down 22% from 2024 and 30% below the 2012 peak. The figures were first reported by the Financial Times.
  • A record 4,137 Japanese companies fully withdrew from China between 2024 and 2026, while only 1,221 entered through subsidiaries, factories or representative offices — the fewest on record outside the Covid pandemic.
  • What it means for investors: Japanese manufacturers are redirecting investment toward India, Vietnam and Thailand, and Japanese financial institutions are expanding in India, which the Economic Times reports they view as a promising destination. For India-focused portfolios, the shift is a concrete demand tailwind for industrial parks, logistics and suppliers.
  • The retreat is driven by U.S. tariffs, rising costs and fierce local competition, a year-long diplomatic freeze, and personnel-safety concerns — with Topix-listed firms' share of profits from China falling below 15%, down from 23% in 2020.

Japanese companies are leaving China in record numbers, as a slowing economy, U.S. tariffs and a diplomatic freeze push businesses to reassess their presence in the world's second-largest economy.

As of June 2026, 10,118 Japanese companies had an established presence in mainland China, according to Teikoku Databank, Japan's largest corporate credit research firm. The figure, published this week and first reported by the Financial Times, is the lowest since the firm began compiling the data in 2010 — a 22% decline from 2024 and a 30% drop from the 2012 peak.

Teikoku's researchers said the data "clearly indicates a shift in Japanese companies' business in China from an expansion phase to a restructuring phase," and warned the withdrawal is likely to continue as firms of all sizes reassess long-held assumptions about investment risk in Chinese manufacturing and the strength of domestic competition in consumer markets.

The numbers behind the exodus

Between 2024 and 2026, a record 4,137 Japanese companies completely withdrew from China. Over the same period, just 1,221 entered through local subsidiaries, factories or representative offices — the lowest number on record apart from during the Covid-19 pandemic.

The retreat shows up in corporate earnings as well. Topix-listed companies saw the share of profits derived in China dwindle to less than 15% so far this year, down from 23% in 2020, according to estimates from Jesper Koll, expert director at Monex Group. Over the same period, the share from the United States rose to 35% from 25%.

Washington is "openly courting" Japanese players to aid its re-industrialization efforts, Koll said, while Beijing has shifted toward a "made in and made by China" model that leaves less room for foreign firms.

Why Japan Inc is leaving

"Investment in China is weathering the perfect storm."

— Martin Schulz, chief policy economist, Fujitsu Research Institute

Schulz links the departure to several converging pressures: U.S. tariffs, growing public resistance to Chinese goods and the development of the Indian market. Teikoku found that about 60% of Japanese manufacturers with production bases in China reported that U.S. tariffs had affected their revenues.

Diplomacy has compounded the economics. Japanese companies have been caught in a dispute between Tokyo and Beijing that has lasted about a year, triggered by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's remarks in parliament about Japan's hypothetical military involvement in a conflict over Taiwan. China responded by restricting exports of critical minerals to Japanese companies, travel between the two countries has fallen sharply, and mainland Chinese tourists visiting Japan dropped 59% year on year in August, according to the Japan National Tourism Organisation. At a major annual travel expo in Guangzhou ahead of China's October 1 National Day, Japanese representatives were absent for the first time.

Personnel safety has become a board-level concern. Several Japanese nationals, including executives at top Japanese firms, were reportedly detained in August over alleged violations of dual-use goods export restrictions. "Japanese firms and their employees increasingly feel unwelcome and unsafe in China," said Jeremy Chan, an analyst at Eurasia Group. An April report from the Japan External Trade Organization showed companies growing reluctant to expand in China.

Where the money is going

The restructuring is not a full decoupling — companies told Teikoku they are trying to reduce reliance on China without abandoning the market entirely. But the direction of new investment is clear: businesses are looking to pivot to India, Vietnam, Thailand and other parts of Southeast Asia after years of intensive investment in China, said Satoru Nagao, a fellow at the Hudson Institute.

"We fed the dragon and it breathed fire."

— Satoru Nagao, fellow, Hudson Institute

India is the standout beneficiary in the narrative. The Economic Times reports that Japanese companies, facing rising competition and geopolitical tensions in China, are weighing investment opportunities in India and its large domestic market — while Japanese financial institutions are expanding their operations in the country, viewing it as a promising destination.

Not every sector is leaving. Automakers, parts suppliers and export-oriented manufacturers are the most likely to scale back, said Kei Koga, a professor at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore — while companies that have localized and can compete with Chinese rivals, particularly medical and precision equipment makers, are more likely to stay.

Beijing's response

China has noticed. A day after the Teikoku report, Vice Premier He Lifeng told a delegation from the Japanese Association for the Promotion of International Trade that China "always welcomes" Japanese enterprises to develop business and share market opportunities. He urged the delegation to "keep to the right course on historical issues" and play a greater role in advancing China-Japan economic and trade cooperation.

What to watch

Teikoku expects the withdrawal trend to continue, which would push the Japanese corporate footprint in China lower still. For markets, the signals to track are the next JETRO business-sentiment survey, Japanese direct-investment data for India and Southeast Asia, and any thaw — or further freeze — in Tokyo-Beijing diplomacy. The restructuring phase, the researchers say, has only just begun.

nri_angle: The pivot benefits India directly: Japanese manufacturers shifting capacity to India feed order books for industrial parks, logistics and suppliers — a concrete demand tailwind for India-focused investment portfolios.
